name: Direction Sense — Which Way and How Far
whatIsIt: Direction-sense puzzles track someone walking North, South, East and West with turns, then ask their final direction or straight-line distance from the start. Draw a quick map with N at the top, add up the North–South moves and the East–West moves separately, and use the right-triangle rule (3-4-5) for the shortest distance.
whyNeeded: Direction sense is a steady scorer in reasoning papers and a real-life skill for reading maps and giving directions. Drawing the path stops you from getting lost in the words.

vocabulary.meaning: North, South, East, West — draw N at the top, E to the right.
How far you end up from the start after cancelling opposite moves.
Turning 90° clockwise (right) or anticlockwise (left) from the way you face.
The straight line from start to finish — the hypotenuse of the E–W and N–S legs.

story.title: Draw the Map, Don't Just Read It
story.text: Dev reads: 'Walk 3 km East, then 4 km North. How far from start?' He tries to imagine it and gets confused. His friend says 'DRAW it — N at top.' Dev draws 3 East, then 4 North. The two legs make a right angle. 'That's a 3-4-5 triangle — the straight line back is 5 km!' Rule learned: always sketch the path with North up, then add E–W and N–S separately.
story.extractedProblem: Walk 3 km East, then 4 km North — straight-line distance from start?
story.answerInStory: 5 km — the East leg (3) and North leg (4) form a right triangle, so the hypotenuse is 5.

visual.caption: Draw the path with North up. 3 East and 4 North are the two legs; the straight-line distance is the hypotenuse = 5 km (a 3-4-5 triangle).

teachingGallery.title: Sketch with N up; add E–W and N–S separately
teachingGallery.note: Opposite moves cancel. Straight distance uses the right-triangle rule on the two net legs.

examples.caption: Equal opposite moves cancel to zero net displacement.

standardMethod.summary: Draw the route with North at the top, total the North–South moves and the East–West moves separately, then find the final direction, and use the right-triangle rule for straight-line distance.
steps: Sketch the path step by step with N up, E to the right.
Add all North moves and subtract South (net N–S); do the same for E–W.
The leftover legs give the final position and direction from start.
For straight-line distance, treat the two net legs as a right triangle (use 3-4-5 or a² + b² = c²).

alternateMethods.name: Turn-tracking with a clock face
alternateMethods.whenToUse: When the puzzle only asks the final FACING direction after several turns.
steps: Start facing the given direction and apply each turn.
Read off N/E/S/W at the end.
alternateMethods.example: Face North, turn right (→East), turn right (→South): now facing South.

workedExamples.problem: A person walks 6 km South, then 8 km West. How far is she from the start?
steps: Net legs: 6 km South and 8 km West (a right angle between them).
She is 10 km from the start.

workedExamples.problem: Facing North, you turn right, then right again. Which direction do you face?
steps: Two right turns = a half turn.

trickPractice.intro: A sketch plus the 3-4-5 triangle solves most of these.

commonMistakes.mistake: Trying to picture the whole route mentally and mixing up the directions.
commonMistakes.fix: Always DRAW the path with North up. A 20-second sketch beats a confused mental image every time.

commonMistakes.mistake: Adding the East and North legs (3 + 4 = 7) for the straight-line distance.
commonMistakes.fix: The two legs are at a right angle — the straight line is the HYPOTENUSE. Use 3-4-5 or a² + b² = c² (here 5, not 7).

teachBackPrompt: Teach a friend to solve '3 km East, 4 km North → how far?' by sketching the path (North up) and using the 3-4-5 triangle to get 5 km. Explain why you don't just add 3 + 4.

revisionCard.summary: Direction sense: draw the route with North up, E right. Total N–S and E–W moves separately (opposites cancel). Final direction comes from the leftover legs. Straight-line distance = hypotenuse of the two net legs (3-4-5, or a²+b²=c²) — never the sum of the legs. Right turn = clockwise 90°, left = anticlockwise 90°.

gameMission.title: Jungle Navigator
gameMission.brief: Map the explorer's path with North up, cancel the opposite moves, and find how far from camp she ends up — remember the 3-4-5 shortcut!

realLifeProject: Give a friend blindfolded step-by-step directions (e.g., 3 steps East, 4 steps North) around a room, then measure the straight-line distance back to start and check it against the 3-4-5 rule.

rememberIt.hook: Draw N-up; straight line is the 3-4-5 hypotenuse
rememberIt.unpack: Total N–S and E–W separately; opposites cancel; distance is the hypotenuse, not the sum.

studentQuestions.q: How do I handle lots of turns quickly?
studentQuestions.a: Track only your FACING with each turn (right = clockwise 90°, left = anticlockwise 90°). Draw the moves for distance, but for 'which way are you facing' just rotate step by step.

studentQuestions.q: When can I use the 3-4-5 shortcut?
studentQuestions.a: Whenever the two net legs are 3 and 4 (or multiples like 6-8, 9-12). Otherwise use a² + b² = c² directly.
